en.title: Street Fighter Director Reveals '90s Anime & Wuxia Fuel His Vision
en.summary: Director Kitao Sakurai dives deep into the vibrant '90s influences shaping the new **Street Fighter** film, from classic anime to martial arts epics. Get ready for a visually stunning ride that honors the game's iconic legacy.
en.body:
Forget grimdark reboots and rote faithfulness; **Street Fighter** director **Kitao Sakurai** is bringing a kaleidoscope of '90s cool to the big screen. In a move that will undoubtedly excite long-time fans and intrigue newcomers, Sakurai has revealed that his vision for the upcoming film is deeply rooted in the vibrant aesthetics of classic anime and the kinetic energy of wuxia cinema. This isn't just about capturing the essence of the game; it's about channeling the specific visual language that defined a generation's entertainment. 

Sakurai’s passion project draws heavily from his childhood loves, citing iconic anime like **Akira** and the **Street Fighter II: The Animated Movie** as major inspirations. The film will even feature striking 2D animated sequences, a deliberate choice to honor the hand-drawn artistry that captivated audiences in the '90s. "We went through a lot of iterations," Sakurai confessed regarding the infamous, gravity-defying hair of **Guile**, a character whose larger-than-life design epitomizes the film’s commitment to embracing the game's unique visual identity. The director aimed for "maximum fidelity," pushing designs to the edge of credulity, a mission statement that promises a film as bold and memorable as its source material.

## A Visual Feast for Fans

The decision to incorporate these distinct influences is more than just an aesthetic choice; it’s a direct nod to the community that grew up with **Street Fighter**. The '90s were a golden age for arcades and fighting games, and the visual flair of that era is inextricably linked to the franchise's enduring appeal. By weaving in elements of **Akira**'s cyberpunk grit and the sweeping martial arts choreography of wuxia films, Sakurai is tapping into a shared nostalgia while also promising a fresh, dynamic cinematic experience. The inclusion of animated segments, in particular, serves as a powerful bridge between the digital world of the game and the live-action spectacle, offering a visual treat that feels both authentic and innovative.

## What to Watch For

With the film set to immerse audiences in a world that celebrates its '90s roots, fans can anticipate a visually rich experience that goes beyond typical video game adaptations. The blend of live-action and animation, coupled with a clear dedication to capturing the spirit of the original games, suggests **Street Fighter** could be a standout entry in the genre. Keep an eye out for further details on the film's release and any additional surprises **Sakurai** has in store.

content_raw: It’s one of the most recognizable silhouettes in video game history. With six-plus feet of beefy muscle squeezed into a tight, sleeveless green shirt, the character they call Guile cut a towering figure over arcade cabinets via his blonde flattop haircut, not least of all because the do reached sizes larger than most men’s heads. This ludicrous-looking sprite is one of the many design choices that made Street Fighter II a staple of ‘90s childhoods, alongside iconography like Blanka’s green-hued skin and Chun-Li’s impossible thighs. And he was among the first things fans saw in the earliest Street Fighter movie teaser, with wrestler-turned-actor Cody Rhodes adorned in an upright, platinum wig roughly the size of a Shih Tzu on his head. “We went through a lot of iterations,” director Kitao Sakurai confides with a weary grin. “ A lot . There was some debate of ‘okay, are we really going to do this?’ But I think at that point, we’re like, ‘ Yes ! We have to do this.’” There were apparently versions of the design more outlandish, scaled to a size where even the filmmaker/lifelong Street Fighter super-fan could concede “that’s too far.” (The biggest being a full six inches taller than the wig in the finished movie.) But in a weird way, getting to that very threshold is a kind of mission statement for the new video game movie: they are going for “maximum fidelity,” and taking it right to the point where it strains credulity. When Street Fighter opens Friday, it will be the second major Capcom video game adaptation of the year after Zach Cregger’s winning take on Resident Evil , and the second this year riffing on 1990s glory days in arcade style tournaments (the other being Mortal Kombat II ). Yet perhaps more than any other video game adaptation in recent memory, Sakurai’s appears to be leaning into the sheer visual lunacy of its game—and away from the instincts of so many Hollywood movies that often seek to ground the absurd of comic books or video games into something approaching reality. “I think that for a lot of years we’ve been getting adaptations that feel like, ‘Okay, what’s the gritty, real world version of this game or IP? How do ground it into the real world?’” Sakurai explains. In fact, that was one of the directions Paramount Pictures was considering when entertaining pitches on a new Street Fighter movie. “I was like, ‘Look, to do that for Street Fighter just feels wrong.’ There needed to be a different approach, and I think that more vibrant, ‘90s, having fun with the [interpretation], that embraces the it was an era when Hong Kong martial artists were going to insane, sometimes dreamlike places that Arnold Schwarzenegger or Sylvester Stallone would never dare venture. “I grew up on Japanese anime and manga, and that was my kind of bread and butter of what I was watching growing up,” says Sakurai. “So I wanted to make a movie that did bridge those gaps.
